extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in aesthetics, character expression, and moral psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Aesthetic and moral criteria for depicting or judging human beauty, grace, and dignity — especially how mind and sensuous nature must relate for expressions to be beautiful, graceful, or dignified. Useful for writers, critics, and students of aesthetics who describe character, gesture, and moral bearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as manifestation of mind through sensuous nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the mind is manifested in such a way through the sensuous nature subject to its empire that it executes its behests with the most faithful exactitude, or expresses its sentiments in the most perfectly speaking manner, ... then we shall see produced that which we call grace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace requires the mind (a super-sensuous cause) to animate the sensuous in a speaking, faithful way. The explanation emphasizes that grace is not mere bodily beauty but the sensuous revelation of moral/mindful principles; produce ease, natural expression, and fidelity of inner sentiment to outward movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty requires a purely sensuous cause
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the purely sensuous cause having its principle in nature which alone can render it beautiful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty (as distinct from grace) is produced when sensuous nature itself — free and not constrained — shapes form; for aesthetic beauty the phenomenon must be allowed to appear free in sensuous terms. When describing or judging form, attend to the autonomy and play of sensuous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid domination by reason or by sensuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “But we should look twice before we should thus qualify ... In the first case, the government would be no more liberal; in the second, it would not be a government at all.” (analogy) — neither the chief making his will outweigh citizens, nor citizens outweighing chief, produces a rightly ordered polity; applied: neither absolute rule of reason nor of sensuous nature produces beauty or grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: (1) Mind dominating sensuous nature (excessive constraint) undermines play and thus beauty; (2) Sensuous nature dominating mind reduces expression to brutish forms. Aim for balanced interplay in depiction: neither forced composure nor unrestrained animality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease is the first requisite of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: “common sense considers ease to be the first requisite of grace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting graceful characters or movements, prioritize natural, effortless-seeming motion and expression. Avoid visible strain, stiff control, or over-precise mechanical gestures; ease communicates freedom and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: No force of will or passion upon the physical nature for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “That which is evident is that neither the will, in the intentional movement, nor the passion, in the sympathetic movement, ought to act as a force with regard to the physical nature which is subject to it, in order that this, in obeying it, may have beauty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: outward form must not betray coercion by will or passion. In writing/critique, mark as un-beautiful any instance where intentional effort or passionate force visibly distorts natural appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical nature must not act as a force over mind for moral expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “... on the other side, nature ought not to act as a force with regard to mind, in order to give occasion for a fine moral expression; for there, where physical nature commands alone, it is absolutely necessary that the character of the man should vanish.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: descriptions dominated by bodily compulsion (e.g., lustful abandon) that erase character and dignity. To achieve moral expression, show that bodily impulses are not the sole drivers of behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three relations between sensuous and reasonable: monarchy, ochlocracy, harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: “We can conceive three sorts of relation of man with himself ... Either man enforces silence upon the exigencies of his sensuous nature ... or ... he subjects the reasonable portion ... or lastly, harmony is established between the impulsions of the one and the laws of the other...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to evaluate characters or expressions: (1) reason over senses (repressive, constrained); (2) senses over reason (anarchical, brutish); (3) harmony (ideal — produces beauty/play). Only the third yields true beauty/grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrained moral sovereignty betrays itself (no beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A mind of this quality makes the physical nature ... feel that it has a master ... Under its stern discipline sensuousness appears then repressed ... This moral state cannot, then, be favorable to beauty, because nature cannot produce the beautiful but as far as it is free...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character's inner life suppresses bodily expression through force, description should show constraint and repression (stiffness, betrayed resistance). This is an anti-pattern for beauty, though it may convey moral rigor or austerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of sensuous domination are ugly and degrading
rubrics_metrics.description: “The eye is watery and languishing, the mouth rapaciously open, the voice trembling and muffled, the breathing short and rapid...the eye...becomes dull, or it protrudes from its socket with I know not what glassy haggardness...the mouth is no longer anything but a simple opening...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete negative indicators: watery/languid eyes, open slack mouth, muffled/gasping voice, short/rapid breathing, coarse colouring of cheeks, trembling limbs. These bodily signs indicate loss of moral autonomy and are to be avoided when aiming for beauty/grace; they can be used deliberately to depict degradation or surrender to appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful expression equals free play between duty and inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: “...that in which the reason and the senses, duty and inclination, are in harmony--will be that in which the beauty of play is produced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to portray characters whose duty and inclination cohere — actions appear voluntary and joyful rather than forced. Depict inner accord so outward behaviour reads as spontaneous, pleasurable conformity with moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to reason must become an object of inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order that obedience to reason may become an object of inclination, it must represent for us the principle of pleasure; for pleasure and pain are the only springs which set the instincts in motion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show moral beauty, represent duty as desirous — show characters deriving pleasure from right action so that obedience feels like inclination, not coercion. This produces genuine harmony and graceful expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous expression of assent cannot be taken as proof of moral merit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus the sensuous expression of this assent, expression that grace offers to us, could never bear a sufficient available witness to the morality of the act in which it is met; and it is not from that which an action or a sentiment manifests to the eyes by graceful expression that we must judge of the moral merit...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution for critics/writers: graceful comportment is not conclusive evidence of moral goodness. Do not infer moral worth solely from pleasing outward signs; inner motives and dispositions may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral perfection is unity of character (virtue = inclination for duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The destiny of man is not to accomplish isolated moral acts, but to be a moral being... virtue is not anything else 'than an inclination for duty.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating morally admirable characters, portray an integrated temperament where inclination and duty are habitually aligned; isolated acts of goodness do not substitute for a noble soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble soul: hallmarks of grace and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the movements which proceed from a noble soul are easy, sweet, and yet animated. The eye beams with serenity ... gentleness of heart would naturally give to the mouth a grace that no affectation, no art, could attain... The voice becomes music, and the limpid stream of its modulations touches the heart.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical markers to write or judge graceful/noble characters: ease and animation in movement, serene bright eyes, natural gentleness of expression, unforced speech, musical voice. Emphasize authentic interior harmony rather than technique or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish beauty (structure) from grace (character)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beauty of structure can excite pleasure, admiration, astonishment; grace alone can charm. Beauty has its adorers; grace alone has its lovers...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction: aesthetic structure (features, form) elicits admiration; grace (moral/character-infused expression) elicits love. In creative work, combine both or prioritize one depending on effect sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace requires union of body suppleness and moral harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: “For grace we require the union of bodily structure, as well as that of character: the body, by its suppleness... the character, by the moral harmony of the sentiments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To depict convincing grace, attend both to physical aptness (supple, responsive body) and to compatible inner character (harmonious sentiments). Either alone is insufficient for full grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity as expression of elevated feeling and moral force
rubrics_metrics.description: “As grace is the expression of a noble soul, so is dignity the expression of elevated feeling... the moral force in man is susceptible of no representation... but it can be represented indirectly to the mind by sensuous signs, and this is actually the case with dignity in the configuration of man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignity should be shown as sensuous signs that indirectly represent moral elevation: measured bearing, controlled gestures, composure. It's not theatrical moralizing but tacit, restrained expression of inner authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will must consult reason before instinct: moral vs physical acts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Well, then, if the will turns towards the reason before consenting to the request of the instinct, it is properly a moral act; but if it immediately decides, without consulting the reason, it is a physical act.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scripting pivotal moments, distinguish choices that arise after deliberation (moral acts) from those that are immediate, bodily reactions (physical acts). The former supports dignity/grandeur; the latter signals lack of moral deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral grandeur arises from resistance to instinct but lacks moral beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus in these sorts of actions we could not find moral beauty, because an action is morally good only as far as inclination has taken part in it, and here the inclination protests against much more than it concurs with it. But these actions have moral grandeur... grandeur is found only there.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to nuance characters: acts of stern self-control (will resisting instinct) may convey greatness and awe but not the warmth of moral beauty (which requires inclination). Distinguish reactions that inspire admiration from those that inspire love.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prevent instinct from dominating, restrain instinct itself
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is but one means of preventing the instinct from restraining the liberty of the will: it is to restrain the instinct itself. Thus we can only have agreement between the law of reason and the affective phenomena, under the condition of putting both in discord with the exigencies of instinct.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical stylistic move: portray characters who cultivate or discipline their instincts so that inclination and duty can later harmonize. This labour of restraint is different from mere repression; it enables later spontaneous concord and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two sorts of bodily movements in affective phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are, then, two sorts of distinct movements, which... arise in man by the instinct of conservation: those firstly which immediately proceed from sensation, and which, consequently, are quite involuntary; then those which in principle could and would be voluntary, but from which the blind instinct of nature takes all freedom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical tool for depiction/critique: separate involuntary sensational movements (uncontrollable signs) from movements that should be voluntary but are usurped by instinct. Dignity and moral expression concern control/modification of the latter; involuntary signs cannot be fully suppressed and may betray interior states.

rubrics_metrics.name: The will's dual character: natural freedom vs moral obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Inasmuch as it is a natural force it is equally free with regard to nature and with respect to reason... but as far as it is a moral faculty it is not free; I mean that it ought to choose the law of reason.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shaping characters' inner conflict, emphasize the distinction: the will can act freely as a natural impulse yet is morally bound to reason. Showing this tension helps explain different outward expressions (dignity, constraint, surrender).
